sec.title: Abstract
sec.p: Candida tropicalis, the most prevalent non-Candida albicans Candida species, is an emerging pathogen forming robust biofilms on medical devices, contributing to biofouling, virulence, and antifungal resistance. In this study, growth conditions for six C. tropicalis clinical isolates (C4, U873, U951, U1179, U1309, U1360) and a standard strain (MTCC-184) were optimized on polypropylene using central composite design-based response surface methodology. The parameters tested included temperature, pH, shaker speed, inoculum size, and incubation time, with biofilm formation quantified by crystal violet, cell viability by MTT, biomass by calcofluor white, and wet/dry weight measurements. Notably, C. tropicalis forms biofilm on polypropylene surfaces, resembling extracellular polymeric substance-rich matrices. Among the isolates, C4, U873, U951, and U1179 fit the CCD model, whereas for MTCC-184, U1309, and U1360, the Johnson Transformation was required to obtain unified optimal conditions. Temperature and pH were the major factors influencing biofilm formation in C4 and U1179, while temperature and incubation time were significant for U873 and U951. A direct correlation was observed between cell viability and biofilm formation, though biomass varied, indicating strain-specific virulence. This high-throughput optimization strategy establishes a platform for antifungal screening, biofilm–material interaction studies, and the development of medical devices resistant to fungal colonization.

sec.title: Key points
sec.p: • Optimized growth conditions of Candida tropicalis biofilm on polypropylene material by RSM
• Four C. tropicalis isolates fit the CCD model; the other three isolates were modelled using CCD–JT
• A direct correlation was observed between cell viability and biofilm with variations in cell mass.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: The rising prevalence of opportunistic fungal infections, especially in immunocompromised individuals, represents a serious global health concern. Invasive candidiasis, caused by various Candida species, accounts for a significant proportion of nosocomial bloodstream infections, often resulting in high morbidity and mortality (Zhong et al. 2022). Factors such as prolonged hospitalization, indwelling medical devices, intensive care admissions, immunosuppressive therapy, and comorbidities like cancer, HIV/AIDS, diabetes, and COVID-19 treatment have contributed to the sharp rise in Candida-related infections (García-Salazar et al. 2022; Ahmed et al. 2022). Candida species are now recognized as major causes of nosocomial bloodstream infections, with candidemia being the third most frequent bloodstream infection in hospitalized patients (Chen et al. 2021).

Among these species, Candida albicans remains the dominant species globally; however, a notable epidemiological shift has occurred toward non-Candida albicans Candida (NCAC) species, such as Candida tropicalis, particularly in Asian countries therefore, declared a high-priority fungal pathogen by WHO (Sharma and Chakrabarti 2023). Emerging pathogens often exhibit higher levels of virulence and resistance to antifungal therapy, which has become a growing concern in clinical practice (Verma et al. 2021). Biofilm formation is a major virulence attribute of Candida species, characterized by organized microbial communities encased in a self-generated extracellular polysaccharide (EPS) matrix. This matrix, with its hydrogel-like properties, provides a hydrated and viscoelastic environment that promotes adhesion to medical devices, fosters the development of protective cell aggregates, and shields microbial cells from both antifungal agents and host immune defenses (Cavalheiro et al. 2018; Sadanandan et al. 2025).

In this regard, polypropylene, a thermoplastic polymer widely used in the healthcare sector, serves as an important substrate for studying biofilm formation. Its properties, including chemical inertness, mechanical strength, low surface energy, hydrophobicity, biocompatibility, and resistance to repeated sterilization cycles, making it ideal for manufacturing medical devices such as syringes, intravenous components, surgical mesh, and implants. However, these same surface characteristics also render polypropylene material prone to microbial adhesion and biofilm formation under clinical conditions (Zielińska et al. 2025; Vachon et al. 2025).

Various tools such as response surface methodology (RSM), Design-Expert, JMP, Minitab, and Statistica are widely used for experimental design and optimization. They enable systematic evaluation of multiple factors and prediction of optimal conditions for microbial growth or biofilm formation (Divyashri et al. 2025; Yogendraiah et al. 2025; Sadanandan et al. 2022a). To optimize biofilm formation under in vitro conditions, statistical modelling approaches are essential. Among these, RSM, particularly the Central Composite Design (CCD), has proven to be a powerful tool that enables systematic evaluation of multiple variables and their interactions, improving optimization accuracy and capturing non-linear effects (Bhattacharya 2021). Though CCD, a robust and flexible design tool, it may provide inconsistent results for incoming rigid and dynamic or adaptive cultures such as C. tropicalis. In order to overcome the inherent limitations of RSM, Johnson Transformation (JT) was used to transform rigid datasets, with a skewed distribution and fit into a normal distribution that helps to retrieve relevant and reliable optimal conditions for the cultivation of C. tropicalis strains.

This study aimed to optimize C. tropicalis biofilm formation on polypropylene material (a widely used medical-grade polymer known for its chemical resistance, biocompatibility, and structural integrity in medical devices such as syringes, catheters, and implantable components) using CCD-based RSM & CCD integrated Johnson Transformation (CCD-JT). The JT normalized non-normal biological data, improving model robustness and predictive reliability. The five main experimental parameters, including temperature, pH, shaker speed, inoculum size, and incubation time, were systematically evaluated to determine their individual and combined influences on biofilm formation. Biofilms were quantified using the crystal violet (CV) assay for biofilm formation, the MTT assay to measure cell viability, and both calcofluor staining and wet/dry weight analysis to estimate total biomass. These five parameters (temperature, pH, shaker speed, inoculum size, incubation time) were selected because they represent the principal environmental and biological drivers of fungal biofilm formation. In biofilm studies, these parameters collectively govern the key environmental and growth-related factors that control microbial attachment, proliferation, and maturation. Accordingly, they are routinely employed to optimize biofilm growth in Candida species under in vitro conditions. Temperature and pH define the physicochemical niche for growth and virulence, shaker speed influences mass transport and shear forces, inoculum size regulates early colonization and cell–cell communication, and incubation time determines progression through the biofilm life cycle. Collectively, these variables allow reproducible formation of biologically relevant in vitro Candida biofilms. This study constitutes one of the earliest comprehensive attempts to optimize C. tropicalis biofilm development on polypropylene substrate using a statistically validated CCD-based RSM. The combined use of CCD and JT provides a robust framework for optimizing fungal biofilms on clinically relevant biomaterials, enabling deeper future to capture insights into Candida biofilm and polypropylene material interactions. Optimization studies not only enhance the understanding of biofilm–material interactions but also support the development of effective anti-biofilm strategies such as conventional antimicrobial therapies, antibiofilm coatings, nanoparticle-based antimicrobials, quorum-sensing inhibitors and enzyme-based biofilm disruption for infection control and materials science (Sadanandan and Yogendraiah 2025; Sadanandan et al. 2023; Ashrit et al. 2022).

sec.title: Microbial cultures
sec.p: Six clinical isolates of C. tropicalis—C4 (sputum) and U873, U951, U1179, U1309, and U1360 (urine)—were collected from male and female patients diagnosed with invasive candidiasis at the Microbiology Laboratory, M.S. Ramaiah Medical College and Teaching Hospital, Bengaluru, India. In addition, a standard reference strain, C. tropicalis MTCC 184/ATCC 750 (blood isolate), was obtained from IMTECH, Chandigarh, India (Yogendraiah et al. 2025; Sadanandan and Manivelan 2021). Ethical approval was not applicable, as the study exclusively employed microbial cultures and did not include human or animal subjects.

sec.title: Growth media and growth conditions
sec.p: For biofilm formation and optimization experiments, C. tropicalis isolates were cultured in tryptic soy broth (TSB) and kept for incubation at 37 °C for 24 h in a shaker incubator operating at 100 rpm. Long-term preservation was ensured by maintaining glycerol stocks at − 86 °C.

sec.title: Growth monitoring and cell count
sec.p: To assess the growth of the C. tropicalis isolates for future use in experiments, optical density was measured at 600 nm using a UV spectrophotometer. Hemocytometry was performed to adjust the cell concentrations to 1 × 106 cells mL−1 and used as stock for further studies.

sec.title: Substrate material
sec.p: Polypropylene sheets were procured from Royal Industrial Stores, Bengaluru, India, and processed into 6-mm discs before placement into sterile 96-well microtiter plates (Axiva Volex) for biofilm assays. Polypropylene was chosen as the substrate material because it is widely used in medical and laboratory devices and is known to support microbial adhesion and subsequent biofilm formation (Islayem et al. 2024; Yogendraiah et al. 2025).

The experimental ranges of the selected biofilm-forming parameters, temperature, pH, shaker speed, inoculum size, and incubation time, were established based on previously published literature. Reported optimum values for each parameter varied across studies; therefore, the lowest reported optimum was selected as the lower limit, while the highest reported optimum was chosen as the upper limit. These literature-derived ranges were used to define the factor levels for the CCD-based RSM, from which the experimental design matrix was generated. This approach ensured that the investigated parameter space remained physiologically meaningful while satisfying the statistical requirements for modelling linear, interaction, and quadratic effects within the RSM framework.

The experimental parameters and their respective ranges were selected based on an extensive review of previously published literature combined with the statistical requirements of CCD. Temperature was selected in the range of 30–37 °C, as C. tropicalis exhibits optimal growth and biofilm development under human physiological temperatures, with enhanced adhesion and extracellular matrix production reported between 30 and 37 °C (Ke et al. 2023; Deorukhkar et al. 2014). The pH range (6.0–7.2) was chosen to reflect near-neutral host-associated environments, which have been shown to significantly influence Candida morphogenesis, surface hydrophobicity, and biofilm biomass (Bizerra et al. 2008; Weerasekera et al. 2016). Shaker speed was evaluated between 75 and 180 rpm to represent low-to-moderate hydrodynamic shear conditions commonly applied in in vitro biofilm models, which directly affect nutrient diffusion and biofilm architecture (Santos et al. 2016; Negri et al. 2016). Inoculum concentration was varied from 1 to 15%, based on earlier studies demonstrating that initial cell density plays a critical role in early adhesion kinetics and mature biofilm thickness (Thein et al. 2007; Ke et al. 2023; Negri et al. 2016). Incubation time was restricted to 18–96 h to capture the early-to-intermediate stages of biofilm development, during which rapid biomass accumulation and extracellular matrix synthesis occur (Deorukhkar et al. 2014; Rezazadeh et al. 2016).

During the development of CCD design matrix, particular care was taken in defining the coded levels (− 1, 0, + 1) and the corresponding axial (± α) points to ensure that all generated experimental conditions remained within scientifically meaningful and biologically relevant limits. The selected ranges were chosen such that the axial points did not deviate beyond the conceptual and physiological limits reported in the literature. The CCD algorithm subsequently generated the intermediate experimental levels by incorporating factorial points, axial points, and center points, enabling robust estimation of linear, quadratic, and interaction effects. Thus, the experimental values employed in this study were derived from literature-supported ranges and optimized through CCD, rather than being arbitrarily selected.

For example: Multiple published studies have reported varying pH conditions supporting Candida biofilm formation. These values were compiled, and then the minimum and maximum reported pH values were chosen as the lower and upper limits. Then, these ranges were entered into the CCD-RSM module of Statistica software. The CCD algorithm subsequently generated the experimental design matrix, including factorial points, center points, and axial points (± α). As a result, intermediate pH levels such as 5.4 and 7.8 represent mathematically defined axial distances rather than manually chosen increments (e.g., 0.5 or 1.0 units). These step sizes are determined by the statistical requirements of CCD to ensure model rotatability, uniform prediction variance, and accurate estimation of linear, quadratic, and interaction effects across the experimental space. A similar literature-based approach was applied to all other biofilm-forming parameters; and the corresponding lower and upper limits, which are used for CCD-RSM optimization, are shown in Table 1.

sec.title: Preparation of pre-inoculum
sec.p: C. tropicalis pre-inoculum was prepared by inoculating a loopful of a freshly grown culture into 5 mL of TSB and incubating overnight at 37 °C under shaking conditions. Cells obtained after overnight incubation were considered to be in the late exponential growth phase. The cell density of the overnight culture was determined using a Neubauer haemocytometer. Based on microscopic enumeration, the culture was adjusted to a standardized concentration of 1 × 10⁶ cells mL⁻1, which served as the inoculum stock for all experiments. From this standardized stock, different inoculum size percentages were prepared according to the CCD experimental matrix. For each of the inoculum size percentage, growth OD and cell count were determined as shown in (Table S1 & Table S2 & Fig. S1 & Fig. S2).

sec.title: Establishing C. tropicalis biofilm on polypropylene material
Experimental validation by CV assay
sec.p: Validation of the optimal conditions predicted by the CCD-based RSM model was performed on polypropylene discs. Biofilm formation was assessed using the CV assay under the identified ideal parameters. The optimized growth conditions for C. tropicalis (C4, U873, U951, and U1179) given by CCD-RSM model are as follows: For C4 isolate—temperature of 33.5 °C, pH 6.2, 36-h incubation, 10.5% inoculum, and shaker speed of 97.5 rpm; For U873 isolate—temperature of 38.7 °C, pH 6.4, 28-h incubation, 12% inoculum, and 99.2 rpm. For U951 isolate—exhibited its optimum at temperature of 36.8 °C, pH 6.5, 41-h incubation, 8.5% inoculum, and 94.1 rpm. For U1179 isolate—temperature of 34.4 °C, pH 6.5, 36-h incubation, 10.7% inoculum, and 75.2 rpm. To confirm accuracy and reproducibility, the experimentally obtained CV values were evaluated against the model’s predicted values.

sec.title: Optimization of C. tropicalis biofilm modeling using Johnson Transformation
sec.p: To obtain statistically reliable and significant modeling outcomes, appropriate data transformation is required to satisfy the assumptions of regression-based optimization models. During transformation, several probability distributions (Gaussian, Weibull, and Rayleigh) are commonly evaluated to assess data behavior; however, normalization itself is achieved using transformation methods such as Box–Cox or JT model. In the present study, an initial Box–Cox transformation was evaluated; however, the obtained lambda value (λ = − 2) deviated substantially from the recommended value of unity, indicating inadequate normalization of the experimental data. Therefore, JT was selected as a flexible alternative capable of effectively normalizing skewed and non-Gaussian datasets. The CCD model profiler tool available in Statistica software provides an integrated platform for correlation editing and best-fit distribution analysis, enabling automatic selection of the optimal JT model. This approach allowed efficient transformation of the experimental data across the defined five experimental levels, resulting in normalized predictor distributions suitable for regression modeling and response surface analysis. In biofilm studies, datasets often deviate from normality due to biological variability. To address this, the JT was applied, converting skewed data to a normal distribution while preserving rank and scale. This ensured statistical validity, along with regression analysis with enhanced reliability of CCD-based RSM outcomes (Yogendraiah et al. 2025; Rathod et al. 2025).

Following transformation, the normality of the datasets was assessed using the Lilliefors, Kolmogorov–Smirnov D statistic (K-S D) test. The calculated statistic (D) was compared with the critical value (Dα = 0.565), and datasets satisfying the condition D < Dα were considered to follow a normal distribution under the null hypothesis. Subsequently, CCD-JT integrated approach ensured statistically valid model fitting and reliable prediction of optimal biofilm formation conditions in a biologically dynamic fungal system.

After the transformation, a capability analysis was carried out to establish optimized target values for each response. These predicted outcomes were then validated experimentally using the CV assay. The experimentally measured biofilm values were compared with the model predictions to evaluate accuracy and confirm that no significant deviations were present.

sec.title: Experimental validation of CCD–JT model
sec.p: We integrated a CCD–JT, which corrects for non-normality by transforming skewed data into a normal distribution and suppressing outlier effects. The optimal conditions predicted by the CCD–JT model were validated through the CV assay on polypropylene material. Experiments were performed in sextuplicates, and the measured CV values were compared with the predicted outcomes to assess reproducibility and ensure the reliability of the model.

sec.title: Quantitative assessment of C. tropicalis biofilm formation under optimized conditions
sec.p: Biofilm formation by C. tropicalis in 96-well microtiter plates under optimized growth conditions on polypropylene substrate material was quantified using established protocols published in our earlier work (Yogendraiah et al. 2025). Biofilm formation, cell viability, and cell mass content were assessed using CV assay, MTT assay, calcofluor staining, and wet/dry weight measurements. Each assay was performed in sextuplicates to ensure reliability.

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: Statistical analysis using two-way ANOVA, followed by Tukey’s multiple comparison test, was used to assess differences between the predicted and observed CV assay values obtained from both the conventional CCD model and the CCD–JT model. All data are expressed as mean ± standard deviation, and sextuplicates were maintained for each of the experiments.

sec.title: JT-based CCD model profiler
sec.p:
In the CCD analysis, the isolates MTCC 184, U1309, and U1360 did not satisfy the model criteria. Their ANOVA outputs showed no statistically meaningful contribution of the tested variables, and none of their effects exceeded the p = 0.05 significance threshold in the corresponding Pareto charts. This limitation is common in traditional CCD approaches, which may exhibit a lack of fit when residual error exceeds observed error. The normality of the JT datasets was evaluated using the Lilliefors modification of the K-S D statistic test. All three isolates (MTCC 184, U1309, and U1360) showed D values below the critical threshold (Dα = 0.565), supporting the null hypothesis and confirming that the transformed responses adhered to the assumptions of normal distribution (Table 3). After establishing data suitability, the combined CCD–JT modelling framework was applied to estimate the most favorable conditions for biofilm formation. The response profiler indicated a common optimal setting for the three isolates, consisting of 34 °C, pH 6.5, 97 rpm shaking speed, 11% inoculum size, and a 35-h incubation period. sec.title: Validation of CCD-JT predictions using CV assay
sec.p:
Confirmation of the CCD-JT model was carried out by assessing biofilm formation under the optimized conditions using the CV assay. As summarized in Table 3, the measured absorbance values were in close agreement with those predicted by the model. Statistical comparison showed no significant deviation between observed and expected responses, confirming that the CCD-JT predictions were accurate, as shown in Fig. 5.Fig. 5
Validation of the CCD- JT for C. tropicalis isolates (MTCC-184, U1309, and U1360) by CV assay

The CCD-JT analysis for the MTCC-184 isolate is presented in Fig. S4. Normality of both transformed and untransformed datasets was supported by the Lilliefors test (p = 0.075; Table 3; Fig. S4A), confirming that the data met the statistical assumptions required for model application. Using these validated datasets, the CCD-JT profiler generated the optimal parameter set for biofilm production (Fig. S4B). Capability analysis indicated a target CV absorbance of 0.350, which was experimentally corroborated by an observed value of 0.354 ± 0.003 (Table 3; Fig. S4C–D), reflecting close alignment between prediction and experiment. The optimal response for MTCC-184 was further described by a second-order polynomial model (Eq. 6). Comparable CCD–JT outputs, including regression equations, were obtained for isolates U1309 and U1360 and are provided in Figs. S5 and S6 and Eqs. 7 and 8.

sec.title: Biofilm quantification of C. tropicalis isolates
sec.p:
After optimizing the growth conditions of C. tropicalis biofilms using the CCD-RSM and CCD-JT models, biofilm formation on polypropylene discs was initially assessed using the CV assay as the primary response variable. Additional quantitative analyses were carried out to verify these trends. For this purpose, cell metabolic activity was determined using the MTT-based viability assay, while total biomass was evaluated through calcofluor staining and gravimetric measurements (wet and dry mass). Based on the CV assay responses, the isolates C4, U873, and MTCC-184 exhibited strong biofilm-producing ability, whereas U951 and U1360 showed moderate formation, and U1179 and U1309 formed comparatively weaker biofilms. A strong direct association was observed between biofilm biomass and cell viability across all isolates, as demonstrated between CV and MTT assay responses (Table S8; Fig. 6), indicating that increased matrix production was associated with enhanced cellular activity.Fig. 6
Quantification of biofilm formation by C. tropicalis isolates on polypropylene surfaces. A Biofilm formation assessment using CV, MTT, and Calcofluor assays to evaluate biomass and cell viability. B Total cell mass determined by gravimetric analysis through wet weight and dry weight measurements

Assessment of cell mass via calcofluor staining and gravimetric measurements indicated that isolates C4 and U873 displayed both high biofilm formation and cell viability, accompanied by considerable biomass production. According to the calcofluor assay and dry weight analysis, isolate C4 remained a high cell mass producer. However, in wet weight measurements, it shifted to the intermediate category. Conversely, MTCC-184 was classified as a high cell mass producer in the calcofluor assay and wet weight analysis, but moved into the intermediate category based on dry weight measurements.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: C. tropicalis is an emerging opportunistic fungal pathogen known for its ability to form dense, structured biofilms that contribute significantly to its pathogenicity, particularly in persistent and device-associated infections (Kojic et al. 2004; Finkel and Mitchell 2011). Within the NCAC group, C. tropicalis ranks among the most commonly isolated clinical species, with especially high prevalence reported across several Asian countries (Sharma and Chakrabarti 2023). C. tropicalis readily attaches to both living tissues and inert surfaces, such as medical devices, where it forms structured biofilm communities that display strong resistance to standard antifungal treatments (Soll et al. 2016; Pereira et al. 2021; Sadanandan et al. 2023).

C. tropicalis forms biofilm particularly on polymeric material such as polypropylene, silicone elastomer, polystyrene, and polycarbonate. The extracellular matrix, rich in polysaccharides, proteins, lipids, and DNA, strengthens adhesion, promotes nutrient exchange, and enhances resistance to stress and antifungal agents. These biofilms enable persistence on medical devices, contributing to infections such as catheter-related bloodstream infections, prosthetic joint infections, and urinary tract colonization (Malinovská et al. 2023; Sadanandan et al. 2022b; Ashrit et al. 2022).

The present study demonstrated pronounced isolate-dependent variability in biofilm formation, as only four of the seven C. tropicalis clinical isolates conformed to the CCD-based RSM model under the tested conditions. This finding indicates that biofilm development in C. tropicalis is not a uniform species-level trait but rather a strain-specific phenotype shaped by intrinsic biological heterogeneity and the ecological niche from which each isolate originates. The clinical isolates used in this study were recovered from distinct physiological environments, including blood, urine, and sputum, which represent markedly different host microenvironments associated with invasive candidiasis, urinary tract infections, and respiratory colonization, respectively. Each anatomical niche imposes unique physicochemical and biological stresses that strongly influence fungal adaptation and biofilm behavior (Sadanandan et al. 2022a; Yogendraiah et al. 2025).

Within the urinary tract, C. tropicalis encounters fluctuating pH, osmolarity, urea concentration, nutrient limitation, hydrodynamic shear forces, and frequent exposure to antifungal drugs, all of which favor phenotypes with enhanced adhesion, stress tolerance, and metabolic flexibility. Isolates recovered from blood are exposed to continuous immune surveillance, oxidative and nitrosative stress, complement activation, and iron restriction, selecting for strains capable of rapid stress adaptation, immune evasion, and robust biofilm-associated protection. In contrast, sputum-derived isolates experience hypoxic conditions, altered carbon sources, mucin-rich environments, and host inflammatory mediators, which can promote alternative metabolic pathways and distinct biofilm architectures. Even within the same sample type, strain-level differences may arise depending on the precise anatomical location, such as catheter-associated urine versus bladder urine or peripheral versus central bloodstream infections (Sasani et al. 2021).

These host-derived stresses profoundly influence host–pathogen interactions and drive adaptive remodelling of fungal physiology. Importantly, such adaptation does not necessarily involve permanent changes in DNA sequence but occurs predominantly through environment-induced modulation of genotype expression. Exposure to niche-specific cues activates differential transcription of genes involved in adhesion, morphogenesis, stress signalling, and EPS synthesis, thereby producing distinct biofilm phenotypes from the same genomic background. Regulatory pathways including cAMP–PKA, MAPK, and HOG signalling coordinate these transcriptional shifts, while epigenetic mechanisms such as chromatin remodelling further stabilize phenotype-specific gene expression patterns (de Souza et al. 2025).

In addition, the nature of abiotic surfaces encountered in clinical settings contributes substantially to phenotypic divergence. Medical devices such as urinary catheters, central venous catheters, endotracheal tubes, and prosthetic materials differ in surface roughness, hydrophobicity, electrostatic charge, and polymer composition, all of which directly affect fungal attachment and biofilm maturation. Surface-dependent sensing mechanisms modulate adhesin expression and cell wall organization, promoting selection of phenotypes optimized for specific materials. Concurrent exposure to antifungal agents further intensifies selective pressure, favoring isolates capable of enhanced matrix production, drug sequestration, and stress-responsive gene regulation (Tseng et al. 2020; Ramage et al. 2006).

Consistent with these adaptive processes, the observed heterogeneity also reflects differences in biofilm-related phenotypes among C. tropicalis isolates. High biofilm-forming strains are generally associated with increased adhesion capacity, pronounced morphogenetic plasticity, and elevated extracellular matrix production, resulting in dense and multilayered biofilm structures. Intermediate biofilm formers typically exhibit moderate adhesion and partial filamentation, leading to thinner and less compact biofilms, whereas low biofilm-forming isolates display reduced surface attachment, limited yeast-to-hyphal transition, and minimal matrix synthesis, producing sparse and poorly organized biofilms. These phenotypes arise from strain-dependent regulation of cell wall composition, morphogenesis-associated genes, and metabolic adaptation pathways (Yogendraiah et al. 2025).

Genotypic diversity further underpins this variability. Distinct multilocus sequence typing clades of C. tropicalis have been associated with differences in adhesion capacity and biofilm biomass, supporting a genotype–phenotype relationship at the strain level (Yu et al. 2017). Differential expression of agglutinin-like sequence genes, morphogenetic regulators such as EFG1, and stress-response genes under host-mimicking conditions has been linked to enhanced filamentation and biofilm stability (Contreras Martínez et al. 2022). Collectively, these findings support a bidirectional model in which the host environment demands specific adaptive phenotypes, and corresponding genotype expression programs are selectively activated, resulting in marked isolate-dependent biofilm heterogeneity. This ecological and regulatory complexity explains why genetically distinct C. tropicalis isolates exhibit divergent biofilm behaviors under identical in vitro conditions and underscores the necessity of accounting for strain-level and niche-driven variability when applying statistical optimization approaches such as CCD-based RSM to fungal biofilm systems (Sadanandan et al. 2022b).

This study aimed to optimize the biofilm-forming conditions of C. tropicalis on polypropylene, a clinically relevant substrate, using CCD-based RSM. Unlike the labor-intensive and limited one-variable at a time (OVAT) method, RSM efficiently evaluates both individual and interactive effects of variables (Sadanandan et al. 2022a; Ashrit et al. 2022). Key parameters, including temperature, pH, shaker speed, inoculum size, and incubation time, were tested at five levels within a CCD framework that incorporated factorial, axial, and center points to capture nonlinear responses. Although temperature, pH, shaker speed, inoculum size, and incubation time are widely recognized as critical determinants of microbial biofilm formation, there are very limited studies in which all five parameters have been optimized simultaneously. Most published investigations examine the influence of one or two variables independently while maintaining the remaining conditions constant. Comprehensive multifactorial optimization of these growth-related parameters is rarely reported, largely due to experimental complexity and increased experimental design requirements.

To date, only a few studies, primarily employing statistical experimental design approaches such as RSM or CCD, have evaluated the combined effects of temperature, pH, shaker speed, inoculum size, and incubation time. Representative examples include the RSM/CCD studies in C. tropicalis (Yogendraiah et al. 2025) and C. albicans, C. glabarata (Sadanandan et al. 2022a; 2022b). In addition, these experimental variables have also been widely employed in RSM-based studies aimed at optimizing yeast biomass and growth conditions by using C. utilis (Li et al. 2009) & Pichia guilliermondii (Mukherjee et al. 2016). Although such studies are not directly focused on biofilm formation, they utilize the same growth-related parameters, temperature, pH, shaker speed, inoculum size, and incubation time, for multivariate optimization; this confirms that while individual parameters have been repeatedly studied, comprehensive multifactorial optimization of all five variables together remains limited in the literature. Collectively, these findings highlight the relative scarcity of comprehensive multifactorial optimization studies in Candida biofilm research and reinforce the rationale for selecting temperature, pH, shaker speed, inoculum size, and incubation time as the principal environmental and growth-related variables governing fungal biofilm development in the present study.

In the current study, C. tropicalis biofilm formation on polypropylene material was successfully optimized using a CCD-based RSM model, revealing that environmental parameters such as temperature, pH, and incubation time significantly influence biofilm biomass compared to inoculum size and shaker speed. Notably, the optimized growth conditions varied among the isolates, reflecting strain-specific adaptability. However, the unified set of parameters derived through the JT demonstrated substantial biofilm formation across all tested isolates, reinforcing the value of transformation-based modelling for generalized predictions (Ponde et al. 2021; Tseng et al. 2020; Tan et al. 2016; Oliver et al. 2020; Chagahi et al. 2024).

Most published studies have primarily examined the individual effects of specific growth parameters on Candida biofilm formation, rather than performing simultaneous optimization of all five variables. To date, there are very limited reports in which all five parameters—temperature, pH, shaker speed, inoculum size, and incubation time—have been optimized together within a single experimental framework. In view of this limitation, additional published studies that investigated Candida biofilm development under defined growth conditions and biofilm characteristics on different polymeric substrates is explained in Table S9.

The material-dependent differences observed in the present study highlight the critical role of surface physicochemical properties in regulating C. tropicalis biofilm development. A higher proportion of isolates exhibited statistically significant model fitting on polypropylene compared to silicone elastomer, indicating enhanced reproducibility on rigid and chemically inert polymeric substrates (Yogendraiah et al. 2025). Similar observations have been reported in recent studies demonstrating that uniform, non-elastic surfaces promote stable fungal adhesion and predictable biofilm maturation, whereas elastomeric materials often support heterogeneous and isolate-specific growth patterns (Atiencia-Carrera et al. 2022; Malinvoska et al. 2023). Polypropylene-supported biofilms in the present work displayed dense EPS matrices and cohesive architecture, consistent with reports showing that hydrophobic polymeric materials enhance EPS retention and intercellular cohesion (Silva et al. 2012). Environmental parameters, particularly temperature, pH, and incubation time, exerted a significantly greater influence on biofilm biomass than inoculum size and shaker speed, corroborating recent findings that these factors regulate fungal metabolism, morphogenesis, and matrix synthesis in Candida species (Dos Santos and Ishida 2023; Atiencia-Carrera et al. 2022). The strain-specific variability in optimized growth conditions observed among C. tropicalis isolates aligns with current evidence of pronounced phenotypic plasticity and adaptive responses under varying environmental and material conditions (Rodrigues et al. 2019). While comparable trends were previously reported in our silicone elastomer-based optimization study (Yogendraiah et al. 2025), the present investigation demonstrates that polypropylene provides improved shear tolerance, faster biofilm maturation, and enhanced model predictability. Therefore, these findings are consistent with recent biofilm literature and emphasize that both substrate characteristics and environmental parameters must be jointly considered for accurate optimization and clinically relevant modeling of Candida biofilms.

JT revealed clear material-dependent differences for C. tropicalis isolates that did not fit the CCD model. In polypropylene however, only three isolates failed to fit the model, including the standard strain (MTCC-184), requiring a slightly lower temperature (34 °C) but a higher shaker speed (97 rpm), a larger inoculum size (11%), and a shorter incubation time (35 h). These trends suggest polypropylene’s rigid, hydrophobic surface demands faster, more energy-intensive EPS production, offering greater reproducibility than silicone elastomer. In contrast, in silicone elastomer material, six isolates required moderate conditions (temperature of 35 °C, pH 6.6, 38 rpm, 7% inoculum, 45 h), reflecting its elastic, heterogeneous surface that supports biofilm under milder shear but with high variability (Yogendraiah et al. 2025). While distinct differences were observed between polypropylene and silicone elastomer substrates in the present study, similar material-dependent variations in Candida biofilm formation have also been widely reported for other polymeric and metallic surfaces. Studies using polystyrene microtiter plates have demonstrated that C. albicans, C. tropicalis, and C. glabrata typically form biofilms under moderate temperatures (30–37 °C), near-neutral pH, and either static or low-shear conditions, reflecting the rigid and chemically uniform nature of polystyrene surfaces (Pierantoni et al. 2021; Tan et al. 2016; Atiencia-Carrera et al. 2022; Sadanandan et al. 2022b). In contrast, biofilm formation on silicone-based materials often occurs under milder shear conditions and extended incubation periods, but exhibits increased heterogeneity and isolate-dependent variability due to surface elasticity and microtopographical irregularities (Tseng et al. 2020). Polypropylene substrates, characterized by their rigidity and hydrophobicity, have been reported to promote stronger adhesion and denser EPS production, frequently requiring higher inoculum density or shaker speed to support cohesive biofilm architecture (Vera-González et al. 2020; Slettengren et al. 2020). Furthermore, studies on metallic biomaterials such as titanium alloys indicate that surface chemistry and energy also strongly influence fungal attachment and maturation, with optimal growth conditions differing from polymeric platforms (Morais et al. 2025). Collectively, these findings highlight that biofilm development by Candida species is governed by the combined effects of material physicochemical properties, surface rigidity, and species-specific physiological adaptability, underscoring the need for material-specific optimization strategies rather than universal growth conditions.

According to a medical market analysis and projection report for 2025 to 2033, polypropylene represents about 39.42% of the medical-grade polypropylene market and is commonly used in syringes, intravenous sets, and diagnostic kits. It offers a rigid, host-like surface that enables more consistent biofilm growth. This uniformity results in a better fit within CCD modeling, positioning polypropylene as a more reliable substrate for high-throughput in vitro screening. In contrast, the same analysis and projection report (2025 to 2030) state that silicone elastomer material accounts for nearly 48% of the medical-grade silicone elastomer market, and is widely used in flexible implants such as catheters, shunts, and pacemaker leads. Its surface properties support strong biofilm growth under relatively mild conditions, making it useful for standardizing individual isolates, although responses may vary across strains (Grand View Research 2024a, b a, b). The comparison of polypropylene and silicone elastomer material properties used in medical devices and their association with biofilm formation is shown in Table S10.

Importantly, in the present study, biofilm formed on polypropylene exhibited robust EPS accumulation and moisture retention. Thick mucilaginous biofilms of C. tropicalis on silicone material have been reported by Tseng et al. (2020). Our findings align with studies showing that surface energy and topography of materials like polypropylene, polycarbonate, and silicone elastomer strongly influence biofilm microstructure (Silva-Dias et al. 2015; Andreani et al. 2017). Notably, polypropylene emerged as a particularly favorable substrate for C. tropicalis biofilm formation as the optimized growth conditions consistently supported reproducible growth and the biofilm formation. EPS structure of C. tropicalis biofilm likely enhances resilience under environmental stress and closely mimics clinical conditions where polypropylene-based devices, such as catheters and syringes, are frequently implicated in biofilm-associated infections (Tseng et al. 2020; Zare et al. 2021; Estivill et al. 2011). The moderate hydrophobicity and surface properties of polypropylene support strong initial adhesion and stable EPS retention, making it suitable for studying biofilm mechanics. Our findings highlight that factors such as substrate rigidity, hydrophobicity, and surface uniformity shape the physiology, reproducibility, and structure of C. tropicalis biofilms, positioning polypropylene as a useful model for both clinical and material science applications (Bezerra et al. 2025; de Souza et al. 2023).

C. tropicalis biofilm formation on polypropylene was assessed using CV, MTT, calcofluor white, and biomass assays under CCD-based RSM optimized conditions. Biofilm formation strongly correlated with cell viability, confirming the presence of metabolically active cells within structured matrices, consistent with earlier findings linking biofilm density to metabolic activity and architecture (Tseng et al. 2020; de Souza et al. 2022). However, variations in total cell mass influenced the relative biofilm-forming capacity across different C. tropicalis isolates, suggesting the contribution of additional biological determinants. These discrepancies may be attributed to strain-level genetic heterogeneity, variable expression of adhesion- and matrix-regulating genes, and differences in yeast cell wall composition, particularly chitin content, which modulates rigidity and surface binding (de Souza et al. 2022). Similar findings have been reported by Zago et al. (2015; Sadanandan et al. (2022a); Ashrit et al. (2022); and Yogendraiah et al. (2025) where they have observed isolate-dependent variability in C. albicans, C. glabarata, and C. tropicalis biofilm formation, even under uniform conditions. Furthermore, EPS production, hydration capacity, and matrix porosity are known to influence both the mechanical stability and metabolic behavior of fungal biofilms (Mancera et al. 2015).

Although C. tropicalis is recognized for its biofilm-forming ability, the precise genetic and phenotypic factors driving this trait are still not well understood. This highlights the need for deeper investigations into biofilm heterogeneity and its clinical implications. In the NCBI SRA database, aside from our submitted C. tropicalis clinical isolates genomes (Sadanandan and Manivelan 2021), C. tropicalis MYA 3404 is the only clinical isolate available, underscoring the need for expanded genomic studies. We are currently working to correlate genotype and phenotype in our sequenced strains and plan to explore cell–matrix binding interactions to better understand the mechanisms of biofilm formation.

In this study, we optimized growth conditions of C. tropicalis biofilm on polypropylene material, demonstrating that the medical-grade polypropylene extensively supports biofilm formation of C. tropicalis. Therefore, it is evident that future research should be in the development of antibiofilm next-generation functional, active, and smart materials. Unlike conventional passive materials that mainly provide structural support but remain vulnerable to biofilm formation, functional materials are engineered with enhanced properties such as improved biocompatibility, surface chemistry, or controlled degradability. Active materials go a step further, interacting with the biological environment by releasing antimicrobial agents or resisting pathogen adhesion through surface modifications. At the most advanced stage, smart materials dynamically respond to physiological cues, such as pH, temperature, or infection signals, by altering their properties in real time to prevent biofilm development and support healing. Current strategies include stimuli-responsive polymers, nanocomposite antimicrobial coatings, and bioinspired surfaces that mimic host defenses (Chaudhary et al. 2025; Ju et al. 2022; Cassa et al. 2024). This shift from passive to active biomaterials not only minimizes device-associated infections but also paves the way for personalized, multifunctional medical devices that actively promote patient safety and extend device lifespan.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: In this study, RSM was employed to optimize the growth conditions of C. tropicalis biofilms on polypropylene material. Key parameters such as temperature, pH, shaker speed, inoculum size, and incubation time, were systematically analyzed to establish statistically reliable biofilm models. Polypropylene material supported more consistent growth responses across isolates, with four out of seven strains fitting the CCD model significantly. For the remaining isolates, the JT method was applied, which enabled us to normalize datasets and determine unified growth conditions with higher reproducibility. Biofilm characterization further confirmed that polypropylene surfaces favored the development of dense EPS matrices, enhancing cohesion and mimicking biofilm resilience commonly observed in clinical device-associated infections. Such findings underline the importance of polypropylene as a standardized substrate for in vitro biofilm modeling and high-throughput screening. Given its widespread use in catheters, syringes, and other rigid biomedical devices, understanding the biofilm dynamics on polypropylene provides valuable insights into device-associated infections. Future strategies should focus on engineering functional or smart polypropylene-based materials that not only retain their structural benefits but also resist microbial adhesion and biofilm development, thereby improving patient safety and reducing the burden of fungal infections.
